chunks: Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar and Muhammad ibn Isma'il from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, all from Safwan from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who marries a woman during her waiting period out of ignorance: is she among those who are permanently forbidden to him? He said, 'No. As for if he was ignorant, let him marry her after her waiting period expires, for people may be excused in ignorance for something greater than that.' I said, 'In which of the two ignorances is he excused: in his ignorance that it is forbidden to him, or in his ignorance that she is in a waiting period?' He said, 'One of the two ignorances is lighter than the other: the ignorance that God forbade it to him, and that he is unable to be cautious with her.' I said, 'So he is excused in the other?' He said, 'Yes, if her waiting period expires, he is excused in marrying her.' I said, 'And if one of them was deliberate and the other out of ignorance?' He said, 'The one who was deliberate is not permitted to return to his companion permanently.'

key_terms.عِدَّةٌ: Waiting period (iddah) after divorce or death

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a marriage contracted during a woman's waiting period due to ignorance?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between ignorance of the prohibition itself and ignorance of the specific status, ruling that a man who marries during the *iddah* out of ignorance is not permanently barred from remarrying her once the period expires. This ruling highlights the Shia juristic principle that *jahala* (ignorance) serves as a valid excuse (*u'dhr*) for temporary irregularities in marriage, contrasting with the permanent prohibition (*haram abadan*) that applies if the act was deliberate (*mu'tamad*). The text further clarifies that if one party acted deliberately while the other was ignorant, the deliberate party bears the permanent restriction, underscoring the importance of intent in marital jurisprudence.
